complete_examples.overview: Complete workflow examples demonstrating the Visual Debug mode handling real debugging scenarios from start to finish.

example.name: debugging_auth_flow
example.scenario: A user reports that logging into their SPA dashboard fails silently. The login page shows no errors, but after submitting credentials, the user is redirected back to the login page instead of the dashboard.
example.user_request: "I'm trying to log in to https://app.example.com/login but after submitting my credentials, it just goes back to the login page. Can you debug this?"

step.description: Set up browser with console and network capture
step.approach: Launch Chromium headed, register console/network listeners, create evidence/auth-flow/ directory. Outcome: browser ready, listeners active.
step.expected_outcome: Clean browser context ready for debugging

step.description: Navigate to login page and capture baseline
step.approach: page.goto('https://app.example.com/login', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' }) Screenshot baseline page state. Collect initial console logs and network requests. Outcome: baseline captured.
step.expected_outcome: Login page rendered. Console: no errors. Network: static assets loaded.

step.description: Fill and submit the login form
step.approach: Fill email and password fields using getByLabel locators. Screenshot before click. Click submit button. Wait for navigation or error with waitForURL. Screenshot after click. Outcome: captured the post-submit state.
step.analysis: Screenshot shows we are back on /login. Console shows: "POST /api/auth/login 401 Unauthorized" Network capture confirms the API returned 401 with body: {"error": "invalid_grant"}. Root cause: the API rejected the credentials, but the client didn't display the error message due to a missing error handler.

step.description: Verify error handling on the client
step.approach: Use page.evaluate to check if the error response is stored in any React state or Vue reactive variable. Check for hidden error elements in the DOM. Outcome: identified that the client receives the error but doesn't render it.
step.expected_outcome: Found a hidden error message div with display:none that should be visible when auth fails.

example.completion: Identified root cause: The login API returns 401 with error details, but the client-side error handler sets a state variable without triggering a re-render. The error message div exists in the DOM but is hidden. Evidence documented in evidence/auth-flow/evidence.md. Handing off to Code mode to fix the state management issue.

key_takeaways.takeaway: Always capture the network response body — status code alone is insufficient. The API returned 401 but the body contained the real error message.
Screenshot alone wouldn't have revealed the hidden error div. Combined console + network + DOM extraction was necessary.

example.name: debugging_layout_regression
example.scenario: A CSS change intended to center the hero title has broken the layout. The title appears off-center on staging but was centered on production.
example.user_request: "After deploying the new CSS changes, the hero title on the landing page is no longer centered. Can you compare production vs staging and find the CSS difference?"

step.approach: Navigate to production URL, capture full-page screenshot. Extract computed styles of the hero-title element. Outcome: production baseline screenshots and style values.
step.expected_outcome: Production hero-title is centered (text-align: center, margin: auto).

step.approach: Navigate to staging URL, capture full-page screenshot. Extract computed styles of the hero-title element. Outcome: staging screenshots and style values.
step.expected_outcome: Staging hero-title is off-center. Computed styles differ from production.

step.approach: Use Qwen3.6 Abliterated vision to visually compare both screenshots. Compare computed style objects. Outcome: identified the specific CSS property that changed.
step.analysis: Visual comparison confirms title is shifted 20px left on staging. Computed style comparison shows: - Production: margin-left: auto, margin-right: auto, text-align: center - Staging: margin-left: 0, margin-right: 0, text-align: left The staging CSS file shows the hero-title class lost its margin properties. Root cause: a CSS selector specificity change caused the centering rules to be overridden by a less specific rule.

step.expected_outcome: Found that a new CSS file loads after the main stylesheet and overrides the centering rules due to cascade order.

example.completion: Root cause identified: The new CSS file (sticky-header.css) loads after the main stylesheet and contains a rule that resets margin on all h1 elements, overriding the hero-title centering. Evidence documented with screenshots showing the visual difference and computed style comparison.

key_takeaways.takeaway: Computed style extraction is faster and more precise than screenshot comparison for CSS value bugs. Use both for complete confidence.
CSS cascade tracing via styleSheets API reveals the source of specificity conflicts.

example.name: debugging_rest_api_flow
example.scenario: An e-commerce checkout flow is broken. The user completes the form, clicks "Submit Order", but the order confirmation page never appears. Instead, the page shows a generic error toast.
example.user_request: "I'm trying to place an order on https://shop.example.com/checkout but after submitting, I just get a 'Something went wrong' toast. Can you trace the API calls?"

step.approach: Register page.on('response') to capture all API responses. Filter for /api/ endpoints. Create evidence/api-flow/ directory. Outcome: network capture ready.

step.description: Navigate to checkout and fill form
step.approach: page.goto('https://shop.example.com/checkout', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' }) Fill shipping form fields. Screenshot before submission. Outcome: form filled, baseline captured.
step.expected_outcome: Checkout page loaded, form fields visible

step.description: Submit order and capture API chain
step.approach: Click submit button. Wait for network idle. Screenshot of resulting page. Review captured API responses. Outcome: API chain documented.
step.analysis: Screenshot shows error toast. API responses show: - POST /api/orders → 201 Created (success) - POST /api/payments → 402 Payment Required (failure) - GET /api/orders/{id} → never called The payment API returned 402 because the test credit card number was declined. The client displays a generic error instead of showing the payment failure reason. Root cause: insufficient error handling for payment failures.

example.completion: Root cause identified: The checkout flow creates the order successfully but the payment step fails with 402. The client-side error handler maps all non-200 responses to a generic message. Evidence includes screenshots of the error toast, the full API response chain, and the payment API response body showing the decline reason.

key_takeaways.takeaway: API chain analysis reveals where in the flow the failure occurs. Without network capture, you only see the symptom (error toast), not the failing step (payment).
Response body capture is critical for payment/debugging flows. Status codes alone don't reveal decline reasons.

example.name: debugging_user_interaction_flow
example.scenario: A multi-step form wizard breaks at step 3. The user can complete steps 1 and 2, but step 3's dropdown for "Shipping Method" doesn't show any options. The dropdown trigger is visible but clicking it does nothing.
example.user_request: "The shipping method dropdown on step 3 of the checkout wizard doesn't show any options when I click it. Steps 1 and 2 work fine."

step.approach: page.goto wizard URL. Complete step 1 fields, click Continue. Complete step 2 fields, click Continue. Screenshot at each transition. Outcome: reached step 3 with screenshots of steps 1-2 working.
step.expected_outcome: Steps 1 and 2 complete successfully. Console shows no errors.

step.approach: Screenshot before clicking dropdown trigger. Click the dropdown trigger element. Wait 500ms for any animation. Screenshot after click. Check console for errors during the click. Outcome: captured the click interaction.
step.analysis: Screenshot after click shows no dropdown menu. Console shows: "TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'map')" Network shows: GET /api/shipping-methods returned 200 with data. The dropdown component received the API data but failed to render because the data format changed (API now returns array of objects instead of array of strings, and the component's .map() call expects strings). Root cause: API response schema changed without updating the frontend.

example.completion: Root cause identified: The shipping methods API changed its response format. The dropdown component calls .map() on the response expecting strings, but now receives objects. The console error points directly to the line number where the .map() fails. Evidence includes screenshots of the non-functional dropdown, the API response showing the new format, and the console error stack trace.

key_takeaways.takeaway: Console errors are the fastest path to root cause for interaction bugs. The screenshot showed the symptom, but the console error identified the exact code failure.
Always capture network responses even for seemingly client-side bugs. The API response revealed the schema change that caused the crash.

example.name: accessibility_audit_complete
example.scenario: A user reports that text on the dashboard is hard to read, especially the card subtitles and status badges. The elements are visible in the DOM but appear nearly invisible to human eyes.
example.user_request: "The text on https://hellodj.celestium.life looks fine in the browser inspector but I can barely read it with my eyes. The subtitles and badges are especially bad. Can you do a full accessibility and visual polish audit?"

step.description: Extract contrast ratios for all text elements
step.approach: Use page.evaluate() to extract computed color, background-color, opacity, font-size, and font-weight for every text element on the page. Compute WCAG contrast ratios and effective contrast (accounting for opacity). Outcome: contrast data for all text elements.
step.expected_outcome: Contrast results showing: - Card background: rgb(45, 45, 68), text: rgb(33, 37, 41), ratio: 1.36:1 - Subtitles at 75% opacity: effective contrast 1.02:1 - Status badges: ratio varies from 1.2:1 to 3.8:1 - Most body text FAILS WCAG AA (4.5:1)

step.approach: Extract font-size, font-weight, line-height, and letter-spacing for all text. Flag text below 14px or with line-height < 1.4. Outcome: font legibility report.
step.expected_outcome: Most text is 14-16px with adequate line-height. Subtitles at 13px with 1.2 line-height are borderline.

step.approach: Identify all elements with opacity < 0.8. Compute effective contrast = raw_contrast × opacity. Flag elements where effective contrast < 4.5:1. Outcome: opacity-adjusted contrast report.
step.analysis: Subtitles at 75% opacity with 4.5:1 raw contrast have only 3.375:1 effective contrast. This is the primary cause of the "barely visible" complaint.

step.approach: Verify alignment consistency across cards (margin comparison within 10px). Check typography hierarchy (h1 ≥ h2 ≥ h3). Verify border/shadow consistency. Detect overflow and truncation issues. Outcome: visual polish report.
step.expected_outcome: Layout alignment is consistent. Typography hierarchy is visually distinct. Border and shadow treatments are consistent across cards. No overflow or truncation issues detected.

step.approast: Resize viewport to 375x667 (iPhone SE), capture screenshot. Resize to 768x1024 (iPad), capture screenshot. Resize to 1280x720 (desktop), capture screenshot. Check touch target sizes (minimum 44x44px). Check for horizontal overflow at each breakpoint. Outcome: mobile verification with screenshots.
step.expected_outcome: All breakpoints render correctly. Touch targets meet Apple HIG (44x44px minimum). No horizontal overflow at any breakpoint.

example.completion: Accessibility audit complete. Key findings: 1. Card text contrast ratio of 1.36:1 is 3.3x below WCAG AA (4.5:1) — PRIMARY ISSUE 2. Subtitles at 75% opacity have effective contrast of 1.02:1 — nearly invisible 3. Status badges range from 1.2:1 to 3.8:1 — some pass, some fail 4. Layout alignment, typography hierarchy, and border/shadow consistency are good 5. Mobile verification passes at all breakpoints with screenshots captured Evidence documented in evidence/accessibility-audit/ with contrast data, screenshots, and task list.

key_takeaways.takeaway: DOM visibility ≠ human readability. An element can pass Playwright's "visible" check (offsetParent !== null) while being nearly invisible due to low contrast.
Always compute effective contrast = raw_contrast × opacity. Opacity is a multiplier, not an additive factor.
Visual polish (layout, typography, borders, shadows) is a pass/fail gate, not optional. Document specific failures with screenshot evidence.
Mobile verification must include screenshots at all breakpoints (375x667, 768x1024, 1280x720) and touch target validation (44x44px minimum).

example.name: theming_verification
example.scenario: A dark mode toggle is not applying correctly. The user clicks the theme toggle button, but the page colors don't change to dark mode. Some elements change, others don't.
example.user_request: "The dark mode toggle on https://blog.example.com doesn't work properly. Some parts of the page stay light even after toggling."

step.approach: Navigate to page in light mode (default). Extract CSS custom properties from :root. Screenshot full page. Outcome: light mode baseline.

step.description: Toggle to dark mode and capture
step.approach: Click the theme toggle button. Wait for theme transition (waitForSelector or fixed delay). Screenshot full page. Extract CSS custom properties from :root. Outcome: dark mode state captured.
step.expected_outcome: Screenshot shows mixed theme: header and sidebar are dark, but main content area is still light.

step.approach: Compare computed styles of elements that changed vs those that didn't. Check which elements use CSS custom properties vs hardcoded colors. Outcome: identified the discrepancy.
step.analysis: Elements that changed: they use var(--bg-color), var(--text-color). Elements that stayed light: they use hardcoded #fff, #333 instead of variables. Root cause: the main content area was built with hardcoded color values instead of CSS custom properties. The theme toggle changes the variables but the hardcoded elements ignore them.

example.completion: Root cause identified: Three components in the main content area use hardcoded CSS color values instead of CSS custom properties. When the theme toggle updates --bg-color and --text-color, those components don't respond because they don't reference the variables. Evidence includes screenshots showing the mixed theme state and computed style comparison showing which elements use variables vs hardcoded values.

key_takeaways.takeaway: CSS custom property extraction via page.evaluate() is the fastest way to identify theme application gaps.
Screenshot comparison shows the visual symptom; computed style analysis reveals the code-level root cause.
